subject: Computer Networking
title: NCP: ARPANET's First Protocol
description: A micro-lesson that makes NCP: ARPANET's First Protocol usable.

hook.text: ARPANET's computers spoke different languages. NCP was the first protocol that let them all communicate.

buildup.text: NCP — Network Control Protocol — handled connection setup and data flow between ARPANET hosts.

discovery.text: It worked, but only on ARPANET. Connecting to other networks required a completely new design.

twist.text: NCP assumed a reliable network. When packets were lost, the protocol broke. That was a fatal weakness.

climax.text: By 1983, NCP was retired and replaced by TCP/IP — a protocol designed to work across any network.

punchline.text: NCP got networking started. TCP/IP made it universal.

quiz.question: Why was NCP eventually replaced?
options: It only worked on ARPANET and couldn't handle packet loss
It was too fast for the hardware
It used too much encryption for the era

details.summary: The Network Control Protocol was ARPANET's first host-to-host communication protocol, operational by 1971. NCP managed data flow between connected computers but assumed the network was reliable. It was replaced by TCP/IP in 1983 when the internet needed to connect diverse networks together.
details.whyItMatters: NCP proved that standardized protocols could enable communication between different computers. Its limitations drove the development of TCP/IP, which made the global internet possible.
takeaways: NCP was ARPANET's first host-to-host protocol from 1971
It assumed the underlying network was reliable
NCP was replaced by TCP/IP on January 1, 1983

faq.question: What were NCP's main limitations?
faq.answer: NCP assumed the network itself handled reliability, which worked on the single ARPANET network. But it could not handle communication across multiple different networks. It also lacked end-to-end error checking, making it unsuitable for the growing internetwork of diverse systems.

faq.question: How was the transition from NCP to TCP/IP managed?
faq.answer: January 1, 1983, known as Flag Day, was the deadline for all ARPANET hosts to switch to TCP/IP. It was a coordinated cutover where NCP was disabled and only TCP/IP connections were accepted. Remarkably, the transition went smoothly with minimal disruption.
